sessions.title: Comfort That Becomes Comfort for Others
sessions.aim: To end the study with Paul's word that the comfort God gives is meant to reach others through us, without making anyone's loss a purpose and without hurrying anyone toward being useful.
sessions.summary:
Four sessions have been about receiving: permission to grieve, words for the pain, an enemy to hate, a hope to lean on. This one turns outward, carefully. Paul calls God "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction" (2 Corinthians 1:3-4).

Read carelessly, that becomes a cruelty: God took your person so you could help other people. Paul never says that. He doesn't give the loss a purpose. He says the comfort you received in it equips you to comfort others, and that is a different claim. The death is still an enemy.

And it can't be rushed. There's a season, sometimes a long one, when a grieving person can only receive. But often, further on, someone discovers that they can sit with another person in the dark without reaching for platitudes, because someone once sat with them. That isn't the meaning of their loss. It's a mercy that came out of it.

keyScripture.why: God "comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" (2 Corinthians 1:4). The purpose Paul names belongs to the comfort, not to the affliction.

discussion.q: Looking back over these sessions, what has comforted you most, and where did that comfort actually come from?
discussion.behind: Start with what people have received before you ask them to give anything. Paul says we pass on the comfort we ourselves received, so name it first. Let people be specific: a verse, a person, a moment in this room.

discussion.q: Some people hear 2 Corinthians 1:4 as "God took your person so you could help others." Why is that cruel, and how is Paul's claim different?
discussion.behind: Protect this distinction. Paul attaches the purpose to the comfort, not to the death. Help the room reject the cruel version firmly while keeping the true one.

discussion.q: Read 2 Corinthians 1:8-9. What does it change to know that Paul wrote these words after despairing of life himself?
discussion.behind: Paul writes, "we despaired of life itself." He isn't speaking from above suffering. Watch for anyone this verse touches closely, and if someone speaks of not wanting to live, follow the care note in the leader's guide.

discussion.q: Has someone who'd been through a loss like yours ever comforted you? What did they have that kind but untouched people didn't?
discussion.behind: Let the room name what a fellow sufferer brings: no platitudes, no fear of silence, the freedom to say "me too" and mean it.

discussion.q: How do you know whether you're in a season of receiving or starting to be able to give? Why does it matter not to rush that?
discussion.behind: Close gently, and go first. Make it plain that the season of only receiving is right and can be long, and that no one here owes anyone comfort yet. Don't press for answers.

objections.objection: Saying God comforts you so you can comfort others is just telling grieving people their loss had a purpose, that God took their person to make them more useful. That's a horrifying thing to say to someone who's bereaved.
objections.response: You're right to reject that, and so does this study. Paul never says God caused your suffering so you could help people. He doesn't make the death an instrument or tell anyone their person was taken for a reason. He says the comfort you received in your affliction equips you to comfort others in theirs (2 Corinthians 1:4). The loss is still an enemy. What has changed is only that the comfort that reached you in the dark has given you something an untouched person doesn't have: the ability to sit with someone else and say "me too" without lying. That isn't a purpose stamped on your pain. It's a mercy that came out of it afterward, which is nearly the opposite.

objections.objection: I'm nowhere near able to comfort anyone. I can barely get through the day. This just adds a burden I can't carry and makes me feel like I'm failing at my own grief.
objections.response: Nothing in this session is a duty laid on you. If you're barely getting through the day, your only task is to receive. There's a season of only being comforted, and it's real and can be long, and rushing a fresh mourner toward usefulness is its own kind of cruelty. What Paul describes isn't a deadline or an assignment. It usually comes later, often years later, and often by surprise. Until then you owe no one your comfort. Let yourself be the one who is held. That isn't failing at grief. It's exactly where you're supposed to be.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who stayed with you in your darkest grief, and what did their presence give you that words never could?
sessions.practice: This week, don't set out to comfort anyone; that can't be forced. Do two things instead, in order. First, receive. Name one specific comfort you've been given in your loss, from God, from Scripture, or from a person who stayed, and let yourself take it in rather than brushing it aside. Second, only if it comes naturally, notice. Is there someone in your life who is now where you once were? Don't ask God what you must do. Ask only whether, and when, the comfort you received might one day reach them through you. Write down what you receive and what you notice, and leave the timing to God.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of all comfort, you've met us in these weeks: in the tears of your Son at a grave, in the words of lament, in naming death the enemy you will destroy, in the hope of resurrection that doesn't deny our pain. We came needing comfort, and you've given it, not all at once and not on our schedule, but you've given it. We don't ask you to make our loss useful, and we refuse the lie that you took them for a reason. We ask that the comfort we've received would not stop with us, and that in your time, and not before we're ready, it would reach someone else still in the dark. Until then, keep comforting us. We're not finished grieving, and you're not finished with us. Amen.
reflection: What comfort have I truly received in my grief, and have I let myself take it in?
Has anyone tried to give my loss a purpose? How is that different from comfort reaching others in its own time?
Where might the comfort I've been given one day reach someone else, and can I hold that as a mercy rather than a duty?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent four sessions almost entirely on receiving. Permission to grieve, from a God who wept first. Words for lament, handed back to us from the Psalms. An enemy named, so our anger has the right target. A hope grounded in an empty tomb, so our grief has a floor under it. Now the study turns outward, and it has to turn carefully, because handled carelessly this is the most hurtful thing in the whole study.

Paul opens his second letter to the Corinthians this way: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" (2 Corinthians 1:3-4).

Look at the danger in that sentence first. It can be twisted into this: God took your person, or allowed the illness or the accident, so that you could become useful, so you could minister to others out of your loss. People say versions of this to grieving people all the time, meaning well, and it's cruel. I reject it, and I hope you will.

Paul doesn't say it. He never assigns a purpose to the loss. He never makes the death an instrument in a plan or tells a mourner their person was taken for a reason. What he says is that the comfort you received in your affliction is what equips you to comfort others in theirs. The purpose belongs to the comfort, not to the affliction. The loss is still an enemy. God didn't take them to make you a better comforter. But the comfort that reached you in the dark, God's presence and the presence of his people when you couldn't stand, has given you something untouched people don't have. You can sit with another sufferer and say "me too" and not be lying.

It helps to know where Paul was when he wrote this. A few lines later he tells them, "we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself" (2 Corinthians 1:8). The man who calls God the God of all comfort had been at the end of himself. He wasn't comforting from above.

And then there's timing, which this session has to guard. There's a season, sometimes a long one, when a grieving person can only receive and has nothing to give. That season is right, and it mustn't be rushed. To tell someone three weeks after a funeral to go and comfort others is its own kind of violence. If you're in the early dark, your only task is to be held. You owe no one your comfort.

But often, further down the road than you can see from here, something happens. You find yourself sitting with someone whose loss is new, and you notice you aren't reaching for platitudes. You aren't afraid of their silence. You can stay in the room with their grief the way someone once stayed with yours. You're not fixing them or explaining their loss. You're simply there, and the comfort you received is reaching them through you. It's almost never planned. Nobody should set out to turn their losses into a ministry. It usually arrives by surprise.

So the study ends without the grief resolved, because it won't be resolved this side of the resurrection. It ends with a God who comforts, and with this: he doesn't waste the comfort he gives. In his time, and never before you're ready, the holding you received may become a holding you offer. That isn't why you lost them. It's mercy brought out of a loss that should never have happened.

scriptureStudy.note: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort." Before Paul mentions comforting anyone, he names God as the source. Any comfort we give is first comfort we received.
God "comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction." The "so that" belongs to the comfort overflowing, not to the affliction being caused.

"For as we share abundantly in Christ's sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too." The comfort is joined to Christ's own sufferings. Grieving people aren't alone in their pain.
"We despaired of life itself." Paul doesn't hide his own darkness. The church's great comforter was himself a man comforted when he was at the end of his strength.
"Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep." The command isn't to fix or explain, only to weep alongside.
"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." Grief is meant to be carried between people, hands under a weight too heavy for one.
The anointed one is sent "to comfort all who mourn." Jesus takes up these words in Nazareth (Luke 4:18-21), so the comfort that passes through us continues his own work.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, follow the thread Paul starts here. It begins with Christ himself, "a man of sorrows" (Isaiah 53:3), who wept at a grave and prayed in anguish in Gethsemane, and who is the one sent "to comfort all who mourn" (Isaiah 61:2). Christians who have suffered have often been the ones best able to console others, not because suffering is good but because the grace that met them was real and could be passed on.

Set that beside our habit of leaving grief to professionals. Counselors and doctors are a gift, and anyone whose grief has turned into depression or despair should see one. But ask what's lost when ordinary believers forget they have anything to give. Jerry Sittser's A Grace Disguised, written after he lost his mother, wife, and daughter in one car accident, is a long reflection on what loss does to a person and what grace can do in it. Ask the group how your church could become a place where the comforted, in time, become comforters, without ever rushing anyone.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group lost her infant son two years ago. She tells you that last month she found herself in a hospital waiting room beside a young mother whose baby was in the same unit hers hadn't survived. She didn't explain anything. She wasn't afraid of the other woman's terror or her silence, because she'd lived inside both. She brought coffee, stayed, and said "me too." She tells the group she still resents anyone who suggests her loss was good for something. It wasn't. Her son wasn't a lesson.

Help the room hear the difference she's drawing. Her loss wasn't given a purpose. The comfort she had slowly received, from many hands, found its way to the next mother in the dark.

Use this to guard the line this session keeps. The loss was never made good. The comfort overflowed anyway, in its own time. Ask the group, gently, where they've received comfort they haven't yet let themselves take in, and leave the rest to God.

memoryVerse.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

leaderPrimer:
Nothing you've led before will quite prepare you for how raw this room can get, and the rawness isn't the danger. The danger is what you'll want to do about it. Someone will weep before the first question is finished, or go silent in a way that fills the room, and everything in you will reach for words that make it stop: the reason, the silver lining, the better place. That reaching is mostly for your comfort, not theirs. The hazard of leading a grief study is comforting too fast, and every platitude you decline to say is a kindness.

The study gives you better ground. It opens with Jesus weeping at a tomb he was about to open, so grief isn't a failure of faith. In the third session, say the word enemy without apology. Paul calls death "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and many people in your chairs have been handed a softer story and felt like traitors for hating death anyway. Give them permission. God hates it too.

Know your room. Someone recently bereaved may not speak for five weeks, and should never be called on. An old grief that was told to hurry up years ago may come out with a force that looks like overreaction and isn't. Someone grieving a complicated loss, an estranged parent, a hard marriage, relief tangled with sorrow, may sit there sure they have no right to grieve. They do. Make room for every kind of loss without ranking them.

Watch for sorrow that has stopped being grief and become danger, the despair that speaks of not wanting to live. Take it seriously, stay close, and get that person to real help that same day (in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline), because a counselor is not a defeat of this study. It is often its best fruit. When grief lasts and begins to take sleep, appetite, or work, encourage a doctor or a counselor, and say plainly that doing so isn't a failure of faith. You aren't a counselor, and nothing here is medical advice.

If you're grieving yourself, you can still lead this. Your honesty about your own loss may be the most helpful thing in the room. Just make sure someone is holding you too.

This study doesn't pretend that true words about the resurrection take away the sting of the grave, and it doesn't resolve its sessions. You don't have to either. You aren't the closure. You're the one who stays in the room while love learns where to put itself now.

faq.q: Is this study going to tell grieving people they should be over it by now?
faq.a: No. It refuses the idea of closure and sets no schedule for sorrow. The first session takes seriously the view that a faithful Christian should rise above grief, and grants that Paul does say we don't grieve "as others do who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). But Paul assumes Christians grieve, and Jesus wept at a grave he was about to open. The study says plainly, more than once, that there's no right way to grieve and no deadline.

faq.q: Does this study think grief is a sign of weak faith?
faq.a: The opposite. The first session is built on the shortest verse in the Bible, "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). He wept at the tomb of Lazarus minutes before raising him. If grief were the opposite of faith, the Son of God would have been an unbeliever at his friend's grave. The study calls grief love meeting death, something God himself did first.

faq.q: Is it really okay to be angry at God about my loss?
faq.a: Yes, and the second session is about exactly this. Roughly a third of the Psalms are laments, and God kept them in his book. Job cursed the day he was born, and God said Job had spoken rightly (Job 42:7). Lament is complaint spoken to God by someone who stays in the conversation, which is different from bitterness that walks away. Jesus himself died praying a lament: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).

faq.q: Why does the study say death is an enemy instead of something natural to accept?
faq.a: Because the New Testament does. Scripture says we are dust and there's a time to die, and the study grants that. But Paul calls death "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26). It entered the world through sin (Romans 5:12) and will be abolished (Revelation 21:4). Your anger at the grave isn't a failure to accept reality. God is against death too.

faq.q: If my loved one is in a better place, why doesn't the study just say that to comfort me?
faq.a: Because comfort offered too fast often shuts grief down, frequently for the comforter's sake. There's real truth in the believing dead being with Christ, and the study says so. But it grounds hope where Paul does, in the event of Jesus dying and rising (1 Thessalonians 4:14), so that grief can weep toward a reunion rather than be told to stop.

faq.q: Does believing in the resurrection mean I shouldn't be grieving so much?
faq.a: No. The hope is about the future and the loss is in the present, and the present is where you live. Jesus knew Lazarus would rise and still wept. The resurrection doesn't erase the goodbye; it makes it temporary, and a temporary goodbye to someone you love can still break your heart. The depth of your grief is a measure of your love, not a failure of your faith.

faq.q: The study says God comforts us so we can comfort others. Isn't that just saying my loss had a purpose?
faq.a: No, and the fifth session guards against exactly that. Paul never says God caused your suffering so you could help people. He says the comfort you received equips you to comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:4). The loss is still an enemy. What can come later is a mercy that grows out of it, not a reason for it.

faq.q: I can barely function. Does this study expect me to go help other grieving people?
faq.a: Not at all. There's a season of only receiving comfort, it can be long, and rushing a fresh mourner toward usefulness is cruel. Your only task right now is to let yourself be held. That isn't failing at grief.

faq.q: What if I've prayed and the grief isn't lifting, or I can't feel God at all?
faq.a: That isn't a failure of faith. Lament exists for seasons when God feels absent, and Psalm 88 ends in the dark with no resolution, yet God kept it in Scripture. Grief can also tip into depression or despair that needs a doctor or a counselor, and getting that help is wisdom, not weakness. God works through physicians and counselors as well as through Scripture and prayer. And if the grief has turned toward not wanting to live, do not wait: in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

faq.q: I'm grieving a complicated loss, someone I had a hard relationship with. Do I even have the right to grieve?
faq.a: Yes. Grief for an estranged parent, a difficult marriage, or a death tangled with anger, relief, or guilt is still grief, and sometimes it's the heaviest kind. The study doesn't rank losses. Complicated love still grieves when it loses its object, often with the added weight of guilt. You have every right to mourn, and the leader is asked to make room for exactly your kind of loss.

faq.q: I'm not sure I believe any of this. Isn't the resurrection hope just a comforting story?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study doesn't ask you to set it aside. It refuses the cheap comforts too; it insists death is a real enemy. And it doesn't ground hope in how badly anyone wants it to be true. It grounds it in a claim about history: that Jesus died and rose, a claim his first followers kept making at great cost. So the question it puts to you isn't whether the hope is comforting but whether it's true, and that's something you can look into.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm grieving myself?
faq.a: Your grief doesn't disqualify you. The study is meant to be led by a fellow griever, not by someone who has mastered loss. Each question comes with a note for the leader, and each session ends in prayer, so you won't be improvising. What you do need is someone holding you while you hold the room. Don't hurry or shame anyone, keep the room safe for every kind of loss, point people toward help without judgment, and read the leader's guide before the first session.

timeline.event: The book of Job tells of a man who loses his children and his health in a single season and meets the loss with raw lament. God finally vindicates him over the friends who defended God with tidy answers (Job 42:7).
The Psalms begin to take shape, many attributed to David. About a third of them are laments, giving Israel words for grief spoken directly to God.

Babylon destroys Jerusalem and its temple. The book of Lamentations grieves the ruined city, and in the middle of it calls to mind that "the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases" (Lamentations 3:22).
Jesus weeps at the tomb of Lazarus before raising him (John 11), and not long after dies on a cross praying the first line of Psalm 22.
Paul writes 1 Thessalonians to a young church grieving its dead, grounding their hope in the death and resurrection of Jesus (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18).
Paul writes 1 Corinthians, calling death "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and soon after 2 Corinthians, which opens by naming "the God of all comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:3).
Augustine writes his Confessions, including his grief at the death of a close friend in his youth and at the death of his mother, Monica, in 387.
Julian of Norwich receives the visions she later wrote down as Revelations of Divine Love, holding together real suffering and the conviction that "all shall be well."
After his friend Arthur Hallam dies in 1833, Alfred Tennyson begins the poems published in 1850 as In Memoriam, a long elegy that refuses easy answers.

In a Christmas Eve letter from Tegel prison, Dietrich Bonhoeffer writes that nothing can fill the gap left by someone we love, and that God doesn't fill it but keeps it open (paraphrased; Letters and Papers from Prison).
C. S. Lewis's wife, Joy Davidman, dies of cancer in 1960. The notebook he kept in the weeks after is published in 1961 as A Grief Observed.
Elisabeth Kübler-Ross publishes On Death and Dying, describing stages she observed in dying patients. The stages help many, and are often misused as a schedule for mourning.
Nicholas Wolterstorff publishes Lament for a Son after his twenty-five-year-old son dies in a mountain-climbing accident.
Jerry Sittser publishes A Grace Disguised, written after he lost his mother, his wife, and his daughter in a single car accident in 1991.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here; I know it took some courage. Before we start, three things. First, you can fall apart here. You can say you're not okay, or that you're angry at God, or that you don't feel any hope right now, and nobody's going to fix you or hand you a silver lining. Second, there's no schedule for grief in this room and no right way to do it. Tears are welcome, silence is welcome, and none of it is too much. You don't have to say anything at all. Third, none of us is here as an expert. Most of us have stood at a graveside with no idea what to say. We're here as people who have lost someone, or love someone who has. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked closely at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, into the quiet house and the empty chair and the hard mornings, because that's where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though nothing's resolved, because grief doesn't resolve on a schedule and I'm not going to pretend it does. This week, take what you're carrying to the God who wept, instead of carrying it alone. Try the practice if you can; if all you can manage is the reflection question, that counts. If something tonight tells you it's time to talk to a doctor or a counselor, hear that as care, not failure. And if your grief has ever turned toward not wanting to live, tell me tonight, or call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any hour. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about confidentiality and about not fixing anyone, and walk slowly through session 1's opening question. Say plainly that there's no schedule for grief.
Week 2: Session 1, The God Who Wept, with extra time on John 11.
Week 3: Session 2, The Permission to Lament, part one: lament in the Psalms and Job, and the difference between lament and bitterness.
Week 4: Session 2, part two: praying the lament psalms aloud together, with unhurried time for anger at God.
Week 5: Session 3, Death Is an Enemy, Not a Friend.
Week 6: Session 4, The Hope That Does Not Deny the Pain.
Week 7: Session 5, Comfort That Becomes Comfort for Others, taking care not to rush anyone.
Week 8: Looking back. Revisit the practices and memory verses, talk about how the group will keep watching over one another, and make sure anyone who needs more help knows where to find it.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the God who wept and the permission to lament.
Week 2: Session 3, Death Is an Enemy, Not a Friend.
Week 3: Session 4, The Hope That Does Not Deny the Pain.
Week 4: Session 5, Comfort That Becomes Comfort for Others, with a short time at the end to look back over the study.

plan: Week 1: Session 1, The God Who Wept.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The notebook Lewis kept after his wife, Joy Davidman, died in 1960, first published in 1961 under a pen name. He writes plainly about the silence of God and about how memory can slowly replace the real person with an image. A companion for sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: Lament for a Son
bibliography.author: Nicholas Wolterstorff
bibliography.note: Short reflections written after the author's twenty-five-year-old son died in a climbing accident, refusing comforts that would make the death or the son smaller. Supports sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: A Grace Disguised: How the Soul Grows through Loss
bibliography.author: Jerry Sittser
bibliography.note: Written after the author lost his mother, wife, and daughter in one car accident in 1991. It neither minimizes the catastrophe nor gives up hope. Useful across the study, especially session 5.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Includes Augustine's grief at the death of a close friend in his youth (Book 4) and at the death of his mother, Monica (Book 9). An early Christian example of grieving without pretending the loss away.

bibliography.title: Lamentations Through the Centuries
bibliography.author: Paul M. Joyce and Diana Lipton
bibliography.note: A commentary (Wiley-Blackwell, 2013) on how Jews and Christians have read and used the book of Lamentations over the centuries. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: Dark Clouds, Deep Mercy: Discovering the Grace of Lament
bibliography.author: Mark Vroegop
bibliography.note: A pastor's guide to biblical lament as a way of staying in conversation with God through loss. Supports session 2.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope: Rethinking Heaven, the Resurrection, and the Mission of the Church
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Argues for bodily resurrection, not a vague spiritual afterlife, as the heart of Christian hope. Supports session 4.

bibliography.title: The Last Enemy: Preparing to Win the Fight of Your Life
bibliography.author: Michael Wittmer
bibliography.note: A short book (2012) that treats death as an enemy rather than a release, ties it to the fall, and sets the resurrection against it. Supports session 3.

bibliography.title: Spurgeon's Sorrows: Realistic Hope for Those Who Suffer from Depression
bibliography.author: Zack Eswine
bibliography.note: Draws on Charles Spurgeon's long struggle with depression. Helpful where grief tips toward depression and the leader needs to point someone toward real help.

bibliography.title: When Breath Becomes Air
bibliography.author: Paul Kalanithi
bibliography.note: A young neurosurgeon's memoir of facing his own terminal cancer. Not a Christian book, but a clear-eyed look at mortality without soft evasions, useful alongside session 3.

bibliography.title: Letters and Papers from Prison
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Letters written from Tegel prison in 1943 to 1945. His Christmas Eve 1943 letter speaks of the gap a loved one leaves, which God keeps open rather than fills. Background for the study's refusal of quick closure.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: On the tenderness of Christ toward people who suffer. A companion to the pastoral posture of the whole study.

furtherReading: A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for anyone who needs a companion writing from inside fresh grief, who doesn't pretend the silence of God away.
Lament for a Son, Nicholas Wolterstorff, for anyone who needs permission to refuse the comforts that make a death smaller, written by a father who buried his son.
A Grace Disguised, Jerry Sittser, for those facing catastrophic loss who want an account that neither minimizes it nor abandons hope.
Dark Clouds, Deep Mercy, Mark Vroegop, for readers who want to learn biblical lament more fully, alongside session 2.
Surprised by Hope, N. T. Wright, for those who want to understand the bodily resurrection hope behind session 4.

glossary.definition: A person's whole response to a real loss: the sorrow, the longing, the disorientation. This study treats it as love with nowhere to go, not a problem to solve or a process with a deadline, and never in itself a failure of faith.

The biblical practice, filling about a third of the Psalms and the whole book of Lamentations, of taking grief, complaint, and even accusation directly to God. Unlike bitterness, it stays in the conversation.
The popular idea that grief reaches a clean ending after which a person has moved on. The study avoids the word, because love doesn't expire and grief keeps no schedule.
The outward expression of grief: weeping, remembering, honoring a loss. Jesus said, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (Matthew 5:4).
Paul's name for death in 1 Corinthians 15:26, the final foe God opposes and will destroy. It frees grieving people to hate the grave instead of making peace with it.
The Christian hope that the dead in Christ will be raised bodily, grounded in Jesus' own rising from the grave. It makes the goodbye temporary, not final.
In the biblical sense, not wishful thinking but confident expectation grounded in what God has done in raising Jesus. It doesn't dry the tears; it gives grief a floor and a direction.
In Paul's sense, the strengthening presence of God in affliction. The grieving receive it first, and in time, never by force, it may reach others through them (2 Corinthians 1:3-4).
Isaiah's description of the servant of the LORD as "a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3), which Christians see fulfilled in Jesus, who wept at a grave and died praying a lament.
The pattern by which people who have suffered and been comforted are often able to console others, not because their suffering was good but because the grace that met them was real.

An attempt to explain why a good God allows suffering and evil. The study warns against offering one at a graveside. Scripture gives grieving people a defeated enemy and a coming end rather than a formula.
The condition of the believing dead now, "with Christ" (Philippians 1:23), before the final resurrection. Real, but not where the New Testament puts the weight of its hope.
The Hebrew word hesed, God's faithful covenant love, which Lamentations says "never ceases" (Lamentations 3:22). It's what the grieving call to mind in the middle of the wreckage.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Grief often gets handled badly in church. People are hurried toward closure, as if tears meant weak faith, or they're given nothing to hold onto at all. This five-session study begins with Jesus weeping at the tomb of a friend he was about to raise. It gives back the language of lament from the Psalms and Job, names death as the enemy God will destroy, sets out a resurrection hope that doesn't deny the pain, and ends with how comfort received can, in time, become comfort given. It won't hurry anyone. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on grief, and before anyone braces, hear this. It won't tell you to get over it, and it won't tell you your tears mean weak faith. It takes grief seriously, it makes room to be angry at God the way the Psalms do, and it never hurries anyone. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. If you're grieving, or walking with someone who is, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). A five-session study on grief, lament, and a hope that doesn't deny the pain. It won't hurry you toward closure or tell you your tears are weak faith.
quoteCards: Jesus knew he was about to raise Lazarus, and he wept anyway.
There's no schedule for grief. Love doesn't expire on a deadline.
Lament is complaint spoken to God by someone who won't leave the room.
Scripture calls death the last enemy. You're allowed to hate it. God does.
The resurrection doesn't erase the goodbye. It makes it temporary, and a temporary goodbye can still break your heart.
The depth of your grief is a measure of your love, not a failure of your faith.
God didn't take them to make you a better comforter. But the comfort that reached you can, in time, reach someone else.
Paul didn't say don't grieve. He said grieve with hope.
